jokes.label: Joke A
jokes.title: The Perfect Field Trip
jokes.joke: I'm a teacher. I took thirty students on the subway and told them, 'If we get separated, stay exactly where you are.' The doors closed with me on the train and all thirty kids still on the platform. I was furious. Ten months of teaching, and they chose THAT moment to listen.

jokes.label: Joke B
jokes.title: Protection Racket
jokes.joke: I got mugged in the subway last week, which honestly felt less personal than getting mugged by the subway itself. Same move every time — guy demands money, disappears for twenty minutes, then shows up acting like nothing happened. At least the mugger had the decency to rob me once. The MTA billed me monthly for it and called it a MetroCard.

jokes.label: Joke C
jokes.title: Parent-Teacher Mafia
jokes.joke: I used to be a middle school teacher, which is basically low-level organized crime without the pension. You run a protection racket on thirty kids for nine months, collect tributes in the form of half-eaten granola bars, and every Friday you have to sit down with the rival syndicate—the parents—and pretend their little guy didn't torch the bathroom trash can. Honestly, the only difference between me and the mob is that Tony Soprano never had to beg for dry-erase markers.

jokes.label: Joke D
jokes.title: Middle School Mob
jokes.joke: I teach middle school. It's basically organised crime with backpacks. The kids run territories in the cafeteria, they shake down the nerds for homework answers, and the other day the ringleader walked up to me after class, cracked his knuckles, and said, "Nice lesson plan you got there. Be a shame if something happened to it during the fire drill."

jokes.label: Joke E
jokes.title: Honesty Unit
jokes.joke: I knew my kid's teacher was getting desperate during the honesty unit. She sent home a note saying, "Please discuss the importance of truthfulness with your children." I signed it, "Dad." The next day she emailed, "Great lesson. Your son turned it in and said, 'My dad says if a lie is believable, it's called customer service.'"

scores.comment: The subway-as-mugger comparison is relatable, but the extended analogy becomes strained. The MetroCard punchline lacks a sharp payoff. An individual mugging does not clearly establish organised crime, weakening prompt fit.

A coherent extended mob analogy with concrete classroom details and effective escalation. The dry-erase marker punchline provides a satisfying contrast, though the teacher-as-gangster premise is familiar and the setup runs slightly long.

Economical construction with recognizable mob dialogue and a concrete closing image. The fire-drill threat is amusing but predictable once the premise is established. Threatening the teacher's authority also introduces a plausible third seed concept.

The honesty-unit setup creates a clear expectation, and the customer-service reversal is understandable. However, the father's role in the exchange is slightly awkward, and the familiar joke about business dishonesty produces more recognition than laughter.
Clean, classic misdirection structure, clear stage voice, mild payoff; familiar 'kids are too literal' territory.
Solid extended metaphor but front-loaded; punchline restates premise rather than topping it, energy dips at the end.
Strong mob-voice pastiche with a real quoted threat as the button; escalates cleanly and lands on the funniest line.
Nice reversal of who's being dishonest, kid's closing line is a genuine quotable turn, tight and well-paced.
Clean, tight stand-up rhythm with a relatable premise, though the punchline is a fairly familiar trope about kids only listening at the worst possible time.
Solid local transit complaint, but a street mugging is more petty crime than organized crime, and the MetroCard punchline feels slightly dated.
Hits both concepts squarely with decent stage voice, but the 'be a shame if something happened to it' mob cliché is too predictable to earn a strong laugh.
Funniest punchline of the batch with a sharp cynical turn, though the middle setup about signing 'Dad' does unnecessary mechanical work.
Clean inversion of the kids-never-listen premise with solid subway staging; final line lands but the turn is the expected one.
MetroCard monthly-bill parallel is sharp, yet the piece uses ordinary mugging rather than organised-crime concepts.
Extended teacher-as-mob metaphor stays concrete and finishes on a specific, usable markers line.
Customer-service-as-lying observation is familiar; narrative framing softens the payoff.
Classic reversal with clean timing; strong final line and clear stand-up voice.
Transit-as-mugger comparison is solid, but organized crime is not clearly used as a concept and the turn is fairly predictable.
Well-developed analogy with several amusing details; consistent escalation though slightly long and familiar.
Clear premise and clean punchline, but the teacher-as-mobster comparison is a common comic route with limited surprise.
